claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed more by kinetic diffusion barriers than by configurational entropy.
A higher density of grain boundaries accelerates elemental segregation.
A higher density of grain boundaries accelerates phase instability.
Controlled annealing can vary grain size and grain-boundary density without changing overall alloy composition.
Atomic diffusion pathways become active at sufficiently high temperatures below the melting point.
Fine-grained nanoalloys possess a higher density of grain boundaries than coarse-grained nanoalloys.
Grain boundaries serve as fast diffusion channels.
Fast grain-boundary diffusion facilitates elemental migration and segregation.
Accelerated elemental migration and segregation lead to phase instability.
Coarse-grained alloys have effectively higher diffusion barriers than fine-grained alloys.
Fine-grained high-entropy nanoalloys will show an earlier onset of elemental segregation than compositionally identical coarse-grained counterparts during high-temperature exposure.
Fine-grained high-entropy nanoalloys will show a greater extent of elemental segregation than coarse-grained counterparts during high-temperature exposure.
Fine-grained high-entropy nanoalloys will show greater phase instability than coarse-grained counterparts during high-temperature exposure.
Lower grain-boundary density in coarse-grained nanoalloys causes slower elemental migration and prolonged phase and compositional stability.
The prediction is limited to temperatures where diffusion is activated while the alloy remains below its melting point.
The prediction applies only before grain growth substantially erases the initial grain-size difference.
